newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian stock market in optimistic mood.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian stock market in optimistic mood.

text.p: The Budapest Stock Exchange (BSE), the second strongest performing bourse in the world this year, looks to the future in an optimistic mood.
"I am optimistic, though we cannot expect such a surge for 1997," Robert Agoston, an analyst at Daewoo Securities, said on Tuesday.
The BUX index soared 170 percent during 1996, beginning in January at 1,528.92 points and ending the year at Tuesday's record high of 4,134.31 points.

Its performance put it in second place to Venezuela on the International Finance Corporation's composite index of emerging market equities for 1996, showing returns in dollar terms of more than 98.3 percent over the year.
Dealers and analysts said that the BSE remained undervalued, adding that the BUX index was likely to be driven higher in 1997 by the same factors behind this year's rally.
"Stronger confidence, new investors and good macroeconomic figures: these three are in the background," Agoston said.

Hungary also benefited from investment funds' strengthening interest in central and eastern Europe, where the developing market economies swung to fast growth after the difficulties of the first years of transition from communism.

Though Hungary's economic growth was below one percent in 1996, the government's austerity programme launched in 1995 and good corporate results fundamentally changed investors' attitudes to Hungarian shares from the end of 1995, they added.
"Two years' positive processes accumulated in the prices," said Robert Forgo, a dealer with MKB Securities.

Hungary launched a strict economic austerity programme in March 1995 to cut its soaring budget and current account deficits but it took almost a year for the results of the programme to convince foreign investors, analysts said.
In March this year the country joined the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development and concluded a stand-by loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund.
The country's image also benefited when six international rating agencies granted an investment grade to the National Bank of Hungary in 1996.
And in addition to these positive developements, Hungarian companies also reported favourable results, analysts said.
"I still do not see a pressure for a turnaround (to profit-taking) as the corporate results underpin these prices," said New York Broker's Attila Gazdag.
Dealers and analysts said that several stocks still had substantial growth potential.

Oil company MOL was likely to lead gainers next year as it was seen improving its annual profits already in 1996 and this process was seen being strengthened by the impacts of gas price hikes on January 1.

The hotel chain Danubius was also expected to extend this year's gains as it improved its position on the market by acquisitions this year, while the 1997 outlook for tourism in Hungary was seen as positive.
Analysts said that the home improvement product maker Graboplast, plastic producer Pannonplast and retail company Fotex could also be beneficiaries of the economic policies planned for next year.

The government said that real wages, which slumped in the last two years, were likely to remain steady or rise in 1996, prompting stronger domestic demand and contributing to better corporate results, while economic growth would quicken to two to three percent.
Futures suggest that the BUX index could rise to around 4,800 points by the end of 1997.

However, analysts and dealers said that macroeconomic developments would continue to influence the bourse strongly and cautioned against the government softening its economic policies too much in 1997, the last year before general elections.
"(For further strong price rises) economic growth is necessary and that the government would not soften its policies in preparation for the (1998 general) elections," Agoston said.
Analysts said that the BSE also needed larger capitalisation for further growth.
